Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.

Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).

2 new polls find Proposition 40 is on track to fail
By Anabel Sosa (https://www.sfgate.com/author/anabel-sosa/) , Senior California politics reporter Oct 28, 2026
People attend a rally against Proposition 40 at the Iron Workers Apprenticeship training center on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, in La Palma, Calif.
Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images
California’s billionaire tax could be headed toward defeat after two separate polls released this week found that Proposition 40 (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/california-billionaire-tax-support-22435258.php) is losing support among voters.
The Public Policy Institute of California released a poll Tuesday evening that found Proposition 40 is on track to fail, with only 46% of voters saying they would vote in favor of the billionaire tax, meaning less than the majority needed to pass the measure are in favor. Another poll from SurveyUSA also found that after leading by 8 points (https://results.surveyusa.com/client/PollTrack.aspx?g=31acdf22-d080-4898-8edd-09896ea966ee) last month, it is now polling at only 44%, a lead of just one percentage point (https://results.surveyusa.com/client/PollReport.aspx?g=b118a915-559d-4669-b870-8a3eae933903).

Yes on 40 signs sit on seats at the “Ballots Over Billionaires” rally on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles.
Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images By the time Proposition 40 first qualified for the ballot in June, California voters were energized by the idea of taxing the rich to salvage healthcare funds, and it was leading in polls for months (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-wealth-tax-polls-2026.html). But voter sentiment appears to be souring in recent months on Proposition 40, possibly because of the massive fundraising effort to sink it. Over $429 million (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767) has been spent by the campaign committee aimed at fighting Proposition 40, and a significant portion is funded by a few billionaire tech executives.
Mark Baldassare, the survey director at PPIC, told SFGATE in a phone call that Bay Area voters are now evenly divided on the issue, with 49% in favor and 49% opposed. Baldassare said that is down 9 points from September, when there was a strong majority in favor.
“The no side has been the dominant voice in the campaign in the last month, and the yes side has not been providing a message as to why people should vote, and I think that’s contributed to this decline,” he said.

Opponents have also put their energy into Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, two other measures that contain language that could nullify Prop. 40 (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/prop40-billionaire-tax-poison-pill-22468923.php) if they are passed.
PPIC’s poll found Proposition 41, which would require audits of special state taxes and prevent any future ones, has 48% of likely voters in support and 49% of likely voters not in support. The PPIC poll found that more Republican and moderate voters are in favor (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf), with 81% of Republicans and 49% of moderates in support, compared with fewer Democrats, with just 28% supporting it.
A slim majority of voters are in favor of another dueling measure, Proposition 42, which would prohibit new state property taxes on personal property, with 51% of voters saying they will vote yes; 47% said they plan to vote no. Gov. Gavin Newsom has endorsed this measure and said that he believes a wealth tax will lead to more billionaires leaving California, thereby leaving the state with a loss in tax revenue.
There is mixed support for Proposition 39, otherwise known as the Voter ID measure, which would require voters to present government-issued photo IDs at polling locations and would invalidate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/) mail-in ballots that do not include the last four digits of a government ID number for the voter.

The SurveyUSA poll found that 49% support the measure, 42% are against it, and 10% are undecided. A news release published with the poll pointed out that opposition tends to rise as elections near and that support for the measure has dipped from last month, when support was 48% and opposition was 38%, making for a 10-point difference.
The PPIC poll found even less support for requiring IDs to vote in California, with 41% of respondents saying they plan to vote yes and 58% planning to vote no. The poll also found a partisan divide, with more Democrats against it and more Republicans in favor.
“Last time, we had nearly the same results as we did this time. What’s interesting about Prop. 39 is the partisan split on that,” Baldassare said. He said he couldn’t comment on the difference in results compared with the SurveyUSA poll.
Leaders of the MAGA movement have advocated for voter ID laws for years, with politicians like President Donald Trump and business leaders like Elon Musk making unverified claims that large numbers of people are illegally voting in U.S. elections.

This month, the Trump administration Department of Justice charged (https://apnews.com/article/california-election-justice-department-60e3dd468f43e0e8a32e6bf69341f189) 28 people with voting illegally last election, out of upward of 27 million registered voters. Democrats have said those people should be held legally accountable but point to the small number of people voting illegally as a signal that the issue isn’t as prominent as claimed.
Beyond the voter initiatives, new polling this week is also giving insight into how politicians will fare on Tuesday. SurveyUSA found Democrat Xavier Becerra has a commanding 22-percentage point lead over Republican Steve Hilton. Meanwhile, incumbent Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a Los Angeles Democrat, appears to be at risk of losing his seat to opponent Angela Gonzales-Torres, a democratic socialist in a Los Angeles House race, according to a third poll (https://www.thedemocracylab.com/ca34) from USC Democracy and Fair Elections Lab. The poll found the two are tied at 34% of likely voter support, but Gonzales-Torres had a lead of 51% to Gomez’s 45% when undecided voters were pushed to pick one candidate. The poll surveyed 423 people in the district Oct. 16-24 and has a 4.8-point margin of error.
PPIC conducted its poll Oct 16-22. It polled 1,086 likely voters, with a 3.8-point margin of error. PPIC defines them as likely voters because they voted in recent elections and said they plan to vote this election.

SurveyUSA is an independent, nonpartisan research company that conducted its poll for KGTV-TV San Diego and the San Diego Union-Tribune. It polled 1,000 people Oct. 19-24, and the survey questions had a “credibility interval” between 3.2 and 5.3 percentage points.

Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images By the time Proposition 40 first qualified for the ballot in June, California voters were energized by the idea of taxing the rich to salvage healthcare funds, and it was leading in polls for months (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-wealth-tax-polls-2026.html). But voter sentiment appears to be souring in recent months on Proposition 40, possibly because of the massive fundraising effort to sink it. Over $429 million (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767) has been spent by the campaign committee aimed at fighting Proposition 40, and a significant portion is funded by a few billionaire tech executives.
Mark Baldassare, the survey director at PPIC, told SFGATE in a phone call that Bay Area voters are now evenly divided on the issue, with 49% in favor and 49% opposed. Baldassare said that is down 9 points from September, when there was a strong majority in favor.
“The no side has been the dominant voice in the campaign in the last month, and the yes side has not been providing a message as to why people should vote, and I think that’s contributed to this decline,” he said.

Opponents have also put their energy into Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, two other measures that contain language that could nullify Prop. 40 (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/prop40-billionaire-tax-poison-pill-22468923.php) if they are passed.
PPIC’s poll found Proposition 41, which would require audits of special state taxes and prevent any future ones, has 48% of likely voters in support and 49% of likely voters not in support. The PPIC poll found that more Republican and moderate voters are in favor (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf), with 81% of Republicans and 49% of moderates in support, compared with fewer Democrats, with just 28% supporting it.
A slim majority of voters are in favor of another dueling measure, Proposition 42, which would prohibit new state property taxes on personal property, with 51% of voters saying they will vote yes; 47% said they plan to vote no. Gov. Gavin Newsom has endorsed this measure and said that he believes a wealth tax will lead to more billionaires leaving California, thereby leaving the state with a loss in tax revenue.
There is mixed support for Proposition 39, otherwise known as the Voter ID measure, which would require voters to present government-issued photo IDs at polling locations and would invalidate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/) mail-in ballots that do not include the last four digits of a government ID number for the voter.

The SurveyUSA poll found that 49% support the measure, 42% are against it, and 10% are undecided. A news release published with the poll pointed out that opposition tends to rise as elections near and that support for the measure has dipped from last month, when support was 48% and opposition was 38%, making for a 10-point difference.
The PPIC poll found even less support for requiring IDs to vote in California, with 41% of respondents saying they plan to vote yes and 58% planning to vote no. The poll also found a partisan divide, with more Democrats against it and more Republicans in favor.
“Last time, we had nearly the same results as we did this time. What’s interesting about Prop. 39 is the partisan split on that,” Baldassare said. He said he couldn’t comment on the difference in results compared with the SurveyUSA poll.
Leaders of the MAGA movement have advocated for voter ID laws for years, with politicians like President Donald Trump and business leaders like Elon Musk making unverified claims that large numbers of people are illegally voting in U.S. elections.

Democrats have said those people should be held legally accountable but point to the small number of people voting illegally as a signal that the issue isn’t as prominent as claimed.
Beyond the voter initiatives, new polling this week is also giving insight into how politicians will fare on Tuesday. SurveyUSA found Democrat Xavier Becerra has a commanding 22-percentage point lead over Republican Steve Hilton. Meanwhile, incumbent Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a Los Angeles Democrat, appears to be at risk of losing his seat to opponent Angela Gonzales-Torres, a democratic socialist in a Los Angeles House race, according to a third poll (https://www.thedemocracylab.com/ca34) from USC Democracy and Fair Elections Lab. The poll found the two are tied at 34% of likely voter support, but Gonzales-Torres had a lead of 51% to Gomez’s 45% when undecided voters were pushed to pick one candidate. The poll surveyed 423 people in the district Oct. 16-24 and has a 4.8-point margin of error.
PPIC conducted its poll Oct 16-22. It polled 1,086 likely voters, with a 3.8-point margin of error. PPIC defines them as likely voters because they voted in recent elections and said they plan to vote this election.

Proposition 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person's wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person's net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state's health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
Proposal
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more "yes" votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 41 or 42 conflict with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effects
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state's General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires.

# California’s Billionaire Tax Slips From 52% Support to 42%
Tech oligarchs have raised over $379 million to fight Prop 40, the one-time 5% tax on billionaires.
By Matt Novak
Published November 2, 2026, 7:51 pm ET
...
California’s Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on all billionaires in the state if more than 50% of voters fill in the box for “yes” by Tuesday.
It’s going to be a close one and may not pass, based on the latest polling.
Back in May, the Public Policy Institute of California found that 54% of California voters said they supported the wealth tax, with 45% saying they’d vote no.
The more recent polling has shown it to be even closer, with a Public Policy Institute of California poll taken Oct. 16-22 showing just 46% saying they would vote yes and 52% voting no.
An even more recent poll by a different organization, the University of California Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, taken Oct. 19-25, shows just 42% saying they’ll vote yes and 50% pledging to vote no.
...
Building a Better California, funded by Google’s Sergey Brin, Eric Schmidt, and several other billionaires, have outspent those who are trying to get Proposition 40 passed 250-1, according to the Washington Post.
...
If Prop 40 passes, about 90% of the money is supposed to be allocated to Medi-Cal, the name for Medicaid benefits in California, according to KQED.
...

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).

People attend a rally against Proposition 40 at the Iron Workers Apprenticeship training center on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, in La Palma, Calif.

California’s billionaire tax could be headed toward defeat after two separate polls released this week found that Proposition 40 (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/california-billionaire-tax-support-22435258.php) is losing support among voters.
The Public Policy Institute of California released a poll Tuesday evening that found Proposition 40 is on track to fail, with only 46% of voters saying they would vote in favor of the billionaire tax, meaning less than the majority needed to pass the measure are in favor. Another poll from SurveyUSA also found that after leading by 8 points (https://results.surveyusa.com/client/PollTrack.aspx?g=31acdf22-d080-4898-8edd-09896ea966ee) last month, it is now polling at only 44%, a lead of just one percentage point (https://results.surveyusa.com/client/PollReport.aspx?g=b118a915-559d-4669-b870-8a3eae933903).

Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images By the time Proposition 40 first qualified for the ballot in June, California voters were energized by the idea of taxing the rich to salvage healthcare funds, and it was leading in polls for months (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-wealth-tax-polls-2026.html). But voter sentiment appears to be souring in recent months on Proposition 40, possibly because of the massive fundraising effort to sink it. Over $429 million (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767) has been spent by the campaign committee aimed at fighting Proposition 40, and a significant portion is funded by a few billionaire tech executives.
Mark Baldassare, the survey director at PPIC, told SFGATE in a phone call that Bay Area voters are now evenly divided on the issue, with 49% in favor and 49% opposed. Baldassare said that is down 9 points from September, when there was a strong majority in favor.
“The no side has been the dominant voice in the campaign in the last month, and the yes side has not been providing a message as to why people should vote, and I think that’s contributed to this decline,” he said.

Opponents have also put their energy into Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, two other measures that contain language that could nullify Prop. 40 (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/prop40-billionaire-tax-poison-pill-22468923.php) if they are passed.
PPIC’s poll found Proposition 41, which would require audits of special state taxes and prevent any future ones, has 48% of likely voters in support and 49% of likely voters not in support. The PPIC poll found that more Republican and moderate voters are in favor (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf), with 81% of Republicans and 49% of moderates in support, compared with fewer Democrats, with just 28% supporting it.
A slim majority of voters are in favor of another dueling measure, Proposition 42, which would prohibit new state property taxes on personal property, with 51% of voters saying they will vote yes; 47% said they plan to vote no. Gov. Gavin Newsom has endorsed this measure and said that he believes a wealth tax will lead to more billionaires leaving California, thereby leaving the state with a loss in tax revenue.
There is mixed support for Proposition 39, otherwise known as the Voter ID measure, which would require voters to present government-issued photo IDs at polling locations and would invalidate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/) mail-in ballots that do not include the last four digits of a government ID number for the voter.

Article continues below this ad
The SurveyUSA poll found that 49% support the measure, 42% are against it, and 10% are undecided. A news release published with the poll pointed out that opposition tends to rise as elections near and that support for the measure has dipped from last month, when support was 48% and opposition was 38%, making for a 10-point difference.
The PPIC poll found even less support for requiring IDs to vote in California, with 41% of respondents saying they plan to vote yes and 58% planning to vote no. The poll also found a partisan divide, with more Democrats against it and more Republicans in favor.
“Last time, we had nearly the same results as we did this time. What’s interesting about Prop. 39 is the partisan split on that,” Baldassare said. He said he couldn’t comment on the difference in results compared with the SurveyUSA poll.
Leaders of the MAGA movement have advocated for voter ID laws for years, with politicians like President Donald Trump and business leaders like Elon Musk making unverified claims that large numbers of people are illegally voting in U.S. elections.

This month, the Trump administration Department of Justice charged (https://apnews.com/article/california-election-justice-department-60e3dd468f43e0e8a32e6bf69341f189) 28 people with voting illegally last election, out of upward of 27 million registered voters. Democrats have said those people should be held legally accountable but point to the small number of people voting illegally as a signal that the issue isn’t as prominent as claimed.
Beyond the voter initiatives, new polling this week is also giving insight into how politicians will fare on Tuesday. SurveyUSA found Democrat Xavier Becerra has a commanding 22-percentage point lead over Republican Steve Hilton. Meanwhile, incumbent Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a Los Angeles Democrat, appears to be at risk of losing his seat to opponent Angela Gonzales-Torres, a democratic socialist in a Los Angeles House race, according to a third poll (https://www.thedemocracylab.com/ca34) from USC Democracy and Fair Elections Lab. The poll found the two are tied at 34% of likely voter support, but Gonzales-Torres had a lead of 51% to Gomez’s 45% when undecided voters were pushed to pick one candidate. The poll surveyed 423 people in the district Oct. 16-24 and has a 4.8-point margin of error.
PPIC conducted its poll Oct 16-22. It polled 1,086 likely voters, with a 3.8-point margin of error. PPIC defines them as likely voters because they voted in recent elections and said they plan to vote this election.

Proposition 40
Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person's wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person's net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state's health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
Proposal
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more "yes" votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 41 or 42 conflict with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effects
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state's General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires.

Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
Two public nonpartisan surveys show Proposition 40 trailing in the final days of voting. Meanwhile, an initiative to require voter ID in California is losing by double digits.
Oct 29, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) speaks at a rally dubbed "Ballots Over Billionaires" at The Novo on Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Khanna for the event in support of Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires, with most of the revenue intended to offset cuts to Medi-Cal and other healthcare services. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12106033/the-political-calculus-behind-newsoms-opposition-to-californias-billionaire-tax) to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40), which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. With days left to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, IGS found just 8% of likely voters still undecided on the measure, which billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12104645/sf-billionaire-chris-larsen-on-ai-this-is-an-incredibly-dangerous-moment) have spent more than $300 million to defeat.
Proposition 39 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39), the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided. PPIC’s poll found slightly stronger support for the measure, but still had it losing.
Support for Proposition 40 appears to be slipping heading into Election Day. Last month’s PPIC poll had a slim majority in favor before the slide this month.
But in the IGS poll released this week, half of likely voters said they will vote no on Proposition 40, while 42% said they are voting yes. That’s a shift from last month, when the IGS poll found 42% of voters against the measure and 45% backing it.
A T-shirt with a campaign message is seen before the start of a rally led by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act at The Wiltern in Los Angeles, on Feb. 18, 2026. Sanders is seeking the support of California voters for a November ballot initiative of an emergency tax on billionaires to help the state’s healthcare system. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Mark DiCamillo, director of the IGS Poll, said the No on Proposition 40 side is clearly benefiting from the huge amounts of money being poured into defeating the wealth tax.
“A well-funded no side campaign usually has the advantage over yes campaigns, just because all they have to do is raise doubts,” he said.
The poll found Proposition 40 backed by strong majorities of Democrats and voters under 40, and opposed by Republicans and voters over 50. Independents are split.
DiCamillo said the disparity between how younger and older voters view the proposed tax is indicative of a growing split that did not used to exist among the California electorate.
From the 2026 Voter Guide
Learn about Proposition 40 and its supporters, opponents, and arguments (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40)
“The generational divide is growing over time, just because the younger set is having a hard time. They can’t afford a house, they can’t reach the American dream,” he said.
“Those are the segments that are now migrating to the Democratic socialists…. They really don’t like the disparity in wealth.”
The fate of the proposed wealth tax will not swing solely on Proposition 40.
Both polls also showed close contests in Propositions 41 and 42, measures put on the ballot by billionaires with language that would nullify the tax if they pass with more votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 41 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-41) would require ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes — those earmarked for a specific purpose. It also would make any new special taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit. Proposition 42 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-42) would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property, and also prohibit most retroactive taxes.
While IGS’s survey showed Propositions 41 and 42 slightly ahead, DiCamillo noted they also found double-digit percentages of likely voters still undecided — and those who have moved since IGS’s September survey have largely turned against the billionaire-backed measures.
“The no side has gained 11 [points] while the yes side is static,” DiCamillo said of Proposition 42.
Proposition 39, the voter ID measure placed on the ballot by Republican lawmakers, has also lost ground since IGS’s poll last month, with the no side gaining 7 percentage points. The survey found Republicans are the only group backing the measure. Likely voters who list no party preference are against it by a 15-point margin in the IGS poll, and majorities of voters in nearly all subgroups — age, race and gender — are opposed.
Sen. Tony Strickland speaks at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, for a press conference highlighting voter signatures in favor of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)
PPIC found similar opposition: That survey has Proposition 39 down by 17 points, with 58% of likely voters saying they will vote no.
DiCamillo said voters appear to be linking the voter ID measure to President Donald Trump’s push for changes to election laws, which are unpopular with Democrats and independents.
“I think Trump is a factor,” he said. “That really is the winning argument: You go after Trump.”
PPIC also polled on Proposition 45 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-45), the ballot measure written by the California Chamber of Commerce to speed up environmental reviews of construction projects. The survey found likely voters split on the changes to the California Environmental Quality Act, with 46% saying they are voting yes and 50% voting no.
The IGS poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19-25, and included 2,787 registered voters. The PPIC poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 16-22 and included 1,728 California adult residents.
Both polls have a sampling error of plus or minus 3%.

California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), with 8% undecided. In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided. It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided. Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass. If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

“These results suggest that neither the advocates of the wealth tax nor those seeking to block future taxes have managed to persuade a majority of voters to their sides,” IGS Co-Director Eric Schickler said. “This may reflect an electorate unhappy with the wealth and power of billionaires but also not sold on a specific solution.”
The poll was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25, 2026, among 2,787 registered voters, of whom a weighted subset of 1,477 had either already voted or were considered likely to vote in the state’s Nov. 3 election. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points for the subset of surveyed likely voters.
It is the second poll this week to find support for the Proposition 40 billionaires tax fading. A Public Policy Institute of California poll Tuesday found that support for Proposition 40 had fallen to 46% from 52% in a September PPIC poll (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/27/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-poll/), while opposition had risen to 52% from 46% last month. That poll also found support slipping and opposition mounting to Propositions 41 and 42, though it found Proposition 42 maintaining narrow majority support among likely voters.
Nearly $400 million has been spent collectively on the three measures, among the most closely watched contests on the state ballot.
Proposition 40 is sponsored by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West (https://yeson40.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24260871789&gbraid=0AAAABC2lkj1e3wEbPnCvZ-bOGGsaK_t-C&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox9nBHZ3OyEIQScw49n6D-MdfgBQwJMBaAh2pUa8NPlFM70x2-SIRhkaAj4cEALw_wcB), which says it would help offset federal Medicaid cuts. It would impose a one-time, 5% tax, payable over five years with interest, on an estimated more than 200 Californians and certain trusts with a net worth — the total value of all assets and property interests worldwide — of $1 billion or more who lived in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Supporters include the California Nurses Association, independent Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna, a Fremont Democrat.
Opponents (https://votenoon40.org/?&utm_medium=paid-search&utm_content=A18&utm_campaign=NoOn40&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24164855903&gbraid=0AAAABEizAVbUeWDtCbY6DbtURFUEQVEPx&gclid=Cj0KCQjw3YvXBhCDARIsAKB-ox_dANRzR4IFRvRvjuHz_CZLLCxIH87pCX5Z85gPQ8lzTiWKkED9jxEaAp18EALw_wcB) include Gov. Gavin Newsom, the California Teachers Association and both candidates for governor — Democratic former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton. They’ve said such a one-time, California-only tax wouldn’t provide recurring new funding and would drive wealthy innovators and job creators, hefty contributors to the state’s income tax revenues, to other states.
Proposition 41 would prohibit new state taxes that exempt their revenues from California’s spending limit and require audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Proposition 42 would prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property, such as financial assets, and limit certain retroactive taxes.
While likely voters were cooling on the billionaires tax, support remained steady for Proposition 3, which would make permanent higher income tax rates on high earners that voters initially approved in 2012, then extended in 2016 until 2030. The higher rates kick in at incomes of $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers, increasing the rate on income above those thresholds from 9.3% to 10.3%. The top rates, which increased to 12.3% from 9.3%, kick in at $743,000 for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers.
The IGS poll found that support for Proposition 3 has held steady at 54% while opposition has edged up slightly to 37% from 34%, and 8% remain undecided.
Support for another statewide measure aimed at limiting local tax measures, Proposition 43, continues to trail opposition, the poll found. Proposition 43 would require two-thirds approval for local special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives, which currently can pass by a simple majority. Special taxes, which fund specific purposes, already require two-thirds approval when proposed by local governing bodies.
The IGS poll found that while support for Proposition 43 grew to 36%, opposition also grew to 46%. In September, 31% were in favor and 40% opposed.
While the poll focused on tax-related measures, it also asked about another closely watched initiative, Proposition 39, which would require voter identification. Support slipped to 37% while opposition grew to 57% with just 5% undecided. In September, 39% were in favor, 52% opposed and 9% undecided.
Proposition 4, which would repeal a state prohibition against public financing for election campaigns, had 41% support and 35% opposition in the latest poll.

The Bottom Line (https://www.cnbc.com/global-cfo-council/) California's Proposition 40: What voters need to know about billionaire wealth tax battle
Published Thu, Oct 22 2026 8:05 AM EDT Updated Thu, Oct 22 2026 12:04 PM EDT

WATCH LIVE (https://www.cnbc.com/live-tv/)
Key Points
California's Proposition 40, the Nov. 3 Election Day ballot measure, would levy a one-time, 5% "wealth tax" on residents of the state with a net worth above $1 billion, an estimated 200-250 billionaire individuals.
While polling from just a few months ago showed a significant edge for the wealth tax, more recent polling suggests the gap has narrowed, and prediction markets expect defeat.
Proponents say the measure could raise as much as $100 billion to fund healthcare in the state after significant cuts resulting from President Trump's tax act, but fears of billionaires leaving the state, highlighted this week by Mark Zuckerberg's invoking of that threat to gain a new stock plan from Meta, are among reasons some economists expect a big government revenue hit.
Opponents include Gov. Gavin Newsom, both candidates to replace him, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who is among leaders of an effort to defeat the measure, with billionaire-aligned groups spending an estimated $1 million per day.

Proposition 40 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/arguments-rebuttals.htm), California's billionaire tax proposal, would authorize a one-time, 5% "wealth tax" (https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/10/21/what-to-know-about-the-billionaire-tax-on-the-ballot-in-california.html) on residents of the state with a net worth above $1 billion. The Nov. 3 Election Day ballot measure has divided politicians, the wealthy, economists, public policy groups, and voters, and it is looking more likely that the vote is headed down to the wire.
The initiative is a major test of the appetite for state-level taxation of extreme wealth — its result, economists say, could shape how other states approach wealth tax policy going forward.
What the latest polls show
In a University of California Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll conducted in September, 45% of likely voters said they would vote "Yes" on Proposition 40, while 42% said they would vote "No."
The results continued a recent shift (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-wealth-tax-polls-2026.html?eafs_enabled=false) in the pollster's data, with the "Yes" edge shrinking from 7% to 3%. In its early August survey, UC Berkeley IGS found 48% of likely voters said they would vote yes. In its polling last March, "Yes" on Prop 40 had a 19% margin, with 52% of those polled expressing support and only 33% expressing opposition. According to its September poll, 13% of voters remain undecided.
A more recent poll conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research for NBC Universal and Telemundo found "Yes" still has a sizable 10% advantage.
Large partisan differences characterize support and opposition to Proposition 40, with Democrats supporting it by more than three to one, while Republicans are opposed nearly eight to one. The views
of non-partisan voters are similar to those of the overall electorate.
While "Yes" continues to have an edge in the polls, prediction markets see Prop 40 going down to defeat by a wide margin. Both Kalshi (https://kalshi.com/markets/kxcawealthtax/will-the-california-billionaire-wealth-tax-initiative-pass/kxcawealthtax-26) and Polymarket (https://polymarket.us/event/ref-ca-blntax-2026-11-03) have the odds of passage currently at under 30%. These markets are not structured with methodologies used by traditional political polling.
How much money the measure could raise
The vast majority of the tax revenue would be used on state-funded healthcare programs, which will help offset healthcare cuts stemming from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/08/tax-break-wealthy-investors-qsbs.html) signed into law by President Trump last year, and which is estimated by the state's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office to cost California "as much as tens of billions of dollars" though it says the impact on general funding will ultimately be determined by discretionary healthcare policy choices made by the legislature.
There are an estimated 200-250 billionaires (https://cabillionairetracker.org/) residing in California, based on tracking of Forbes data and other sources.
Alan Auerbach, economics professor at Berkeley, said the concentration of wealth among a very small number of Californians is a key sticking point of the proposal. On the estimates of around 200 individuals, he said, "Even among this number, wealth is very concentrated among the [very] wealthiest."
